requirement: All clinician, clinic-administrator, support and cloud-administrator accounts must use multi-factor authentication; prefer number-matching or phishing-resistant methods and limit repeated prompts.
Patients must be offered MFA at enrolment; MFA must be required for high-risk actions (changing contact details, exporting data).
Login endpoints must throttle repeated failures per account and per source, and raise an alert on credential-stuffing patterns.
Every API request that reads or changes a patient object must be authorised on the server against the caller's identity (patient owns the record, or clinician is assigned).
Maintain one documented role-and-permission model following least privilege, and review access rights at a defined interval.
Validate all incoming readings (format, plausible range, timestamp, binding to an authenticated device identity) and reject malformed or duplicate data.
Changes to alert thresholds must require an authorised role, be recorded with who/what/when, and be visible to the responsible clinician.
The device must verify a cryptographic signature on every firmware image before installing it, and refuse older versions (rollback protection).
Firmware-signing keys must be stored in a protected key-management service or hardware module, with restricted, logged access.
Each device must have a unique credential held in protected storage on the device, and Aurelia must be able to revoke a device credential.
Device-to-phone pairing must use an authenticated and encrypted Bluetooth Low Energy connection.
The EHR integration must use per-customer, short-lived or regularly rotated credentials held in a secrets manager, with scope limited to the data needed.
Notification content must contain no health detail beyond a generic prompt to open the app.
Define a secure cloud configuration baseline, forbid public data stores by default, and scan for misconfiguration on a schedule.
Cloud administrators must use separate privileged accounts with MFA, time-limited elevation and full logging.
Support access to patient data must be just-in-time, tied to a ticket, masked by default, fully logged and periodically reviewed.
Authentication events, patient-data access, administrative actions and configuration changes must be logged centrally with user, time, source and outcome, and protected from alteration.
Define detection rules and a named owner who reviews alerts and a sample of logs on a fixed schedule.
Maintain a documented incident-response plan with roles, escalation and decision points, and rehearse it at least annually.
Protect public endpoints with rate limiting and capacity monitoring, and monitor that alerts are actually delivered.
Back up patient data with encrypted, isolated copies and test restoration on a schedule.
Define a documented break-glass procedure for identity-provider outage and assess the provider as a supplier.
Follow a secure development lifecycle: code review, static analysis, dependency scanning, safe error handling and a patching timeline for known vulnerabilities.
Use TLS for all internet traffic and short-lived session tokens that are revoked on logout, password change and suspected compromise.
